newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan may pay first ex-Korean 'comfort woman'.
newsitem.headline: Japan may pay first ex-Korean 'comfort woman'.

text.p: Japan may soon pay "atonement money" to a Korean woman forced to serve as a sex slave for the Japanese army during World War Two, the first time a Korean has agreed to accept compensation, officials of a special fund said on Wednesday.

With all other so-called Korean "comfort women" rejecting the controversial Japanese payment, the 75-year old woman, identified only by her pre-war Japanese name of Kimiko Kaneda, may become the first Korean to accept the money, officials of the private Asian Women's Fund said.

Japan has rejected paying wartime compensation to former "comfort women" on grounds that various peace treaties have settled war reparations. Instead, the Japanese government set up the Asian Women's Fund to disburse "atonement money".
Only eight former "comfort women," all from the Philippines, have so far accepted such payments from the fund.
Officials of the government-backed, Tokyo-based fund said on Wednesday the organisation was discussing how to meet the Korean woman's demands with various government ministries.

The woman said she would accept a total of five million yen ($44,200). Of that, two million yen ($17,600) would come from the fund in the form of a one-time cash payment and three million yen ($26,500) in medical and welfare aid in installments from the Japanese government, they said.
The fund official said she could become the first of 160 women in South Korea eligible for such payments.
"We would like to handle it in accordance with her request and conditions surrounding her," a fund spokesman told Reuters.
The "comfort women" affair is one of Japan's darkest chapters in its history before the end of World War Two.

After being sued by former sex-slaves, the Japanese government finally admitted in August 1993 that it was the army, and not private brothel owners as it had maintained for decades, that kidnapped or tricked women into sex slavery.
Even then, the government refused to compensate the women, saying all such demands were dealt with in the 1952 San Francisco Peace Treaty and related bilateral pacts.

Asian governments such as China and South Korea have accepted Tokyo's stance on state-to-state reparations, but have said they would not stop their citizens from seeking redress from Japan individually.

Historians say up to 200,000 women -- mostly Koreans but also from the Philippines, Indonesia, China and the Netherlands -- were pressed into sexual servitude in front-line brothels as Japanese forces swept through East Asia.
